---
title: "Same Data, Different Estimators"
date: "2026-05-13"
---

## One panel, several estimators

Here I use the BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics county file to compare a
few panel estimators. The data are public, large enough to be interesting, and
have a natural COVID example: stay-at-home orders in April 2020.

The point is to keep the data fixed. If I change the data every time I change
the estimator, then it is hard to know whether the result changed because of
the estimator or because of the sample. So here I build one panel and pass the
same outcome matrix to several methods.

The setup follows the application in Shen, Song, and Abadie:

| quantity | value |
| --- | ---: |
| outcome | county unemployment rate |
| data source | BLS LAUS county flat file |
| pre-period | January 2008 to March 2020 |
| post-period | April 2020 |
| control states | Arkansas, Iowa, Nebraska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah, Wyoming |
| treated units | counties in stay-at-home-order states |
| excluded units | Alaska and District of Columbia |
| control counties | 438 |
| treated counties | 2,674 |
| pre-treatment months | 147 |

The paper reports an ATT of about 5.06 percentage points. With the current BLS
flat file and the code below, `MSC.jl` builds the same-sized panel and gives
4.9552 under the default bounded solver settings.

## Construct the panel once

The key is to build one common panel first. The matrix has controls first,
treated units second, pre-treatment months first, and April 2020 as the only
post-treatment month.

The `MSC.jl` example script contains the data-preparation helper, so we can
reuse it rather than duplicating parsing logic:

```julia
using MSC
using SynthDiD
using Statistics

include("/home/xao/projects/software/MSC.jl/examples/03_covid_sah_orders.jl")

df = load_laus_county_panel(find_laus_county_file())
panel = MSC.panel_matrices(df, :county, :month, :unemployment_rate, :D)

Y = Matrix{Float64}(panel.Y)
N0 = panel.N0
T0 = panel.T0
```

Here `N0 = 438`, `size(Y, 1) - N0 = 2674`, and `T0 = 147`.

### A DuckDB version of the same panel step

The raw LAUS county file is large enough that I want to separate two jobs:

1. use DuckDB to scan, filter, complete-case-check, and order the flat file;
2. hand the resulting common panel to the estimators.

The estimators do not need to know that DuckDB was used. They still receive the
same `DataFrame`, then the same `Y`, `N0`, and `T0`.

```julia
using DataFrames
using DBInterface
using DuckDB
using MSC

const CONTROL_STATE_FIPS = ("05", "19", "31", "38", "46", "49", "56")
const EXCLUDED_STATE_FIPS = ("02", "11")

sqlpath(path) = replace(path, "'" => "''")

function load_laus_county_panel_duckdb(
    laus_dir;
    start_year = 2008,
    start_month = 1,
    end_year = 2020,
    end_month = 4,
)
    county_path = sqlpath(joinpath(laus_dir, "la.data.64.County"))
    start_idx = 12 * start_year + start_month
    end_idx = 12 * end_year + end_month
    controls = join(["'$x'" for x in CONTROL_STATE_FIPS], ", ")
    excluded = join(["'$x'" for x in EXCLUDED_STATE_FIPS], ", ")

    con = DBInterface.connect(DuckDB.DB())

    DataFrame(DBInterface.execute(con, """
    WITH raw AS (
        SELECT
            trim(series_id) AS county,
            substr(trim(series_id), 6, 2) AS state_fips,
            CAST(year AS INTEGER) AS year,
            CAST(substr(period, 2, 2) AS INTEGER) AS month_num,
            12 * CAST(year AS INTEGER) + CAST(substr(period, 2, 2) AS INTEGER) AS month_index,
            try_cast(trim(value) AS DOUBLE) AS unemployment_rate
        FROM read_csv_auto('$county_path', delim='\t', header=true, all_varchar=true)
        WHERE starts_with(trim(series_id), 'LAUCN')
          AND ends_with(trim(series_id), '03')
          AND period != 'M13'
    ), filtered AS (
        SELECT *
        FROM raw
        WHERE state_fips NOT IN ($excluded)
          AND month_index BETWEEN $start_idx AND $end_idx
          AND unemployment_rate IS NOT NULL
    ), complete_counties AS (
        SELECT county
        FROM filtered
        GROUP BY county
        HAVING count(*) = (SELECT count(DISTINCT month_index) FROM filtered)
    )
    SELECT
        f.county,
        CAST(f.year AS VARCHAR) || '-' || lpad(CAST(f.month_num AS VARCHAR), 2, '0') AS month,
        f.unemployment_rate,
        CASE WHEN f.state_fips IN ($controls) THEN 0.0 ELSE 1.0 END
          * CASE WHEN f.month_index = $end_idx THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END AS D,
        f.state_fips
    FROM filtered f
    JOIN complete_counties c USING (county)
    ORDER BY
        CASE WHEN f.state_fips IN ($controls) THEN 0 ELSE 1 END,
        f.county,
        f.month_index
    """))
end

df = load_laus_county_panel_duckdb(expanduser("~/projects/data/laus"))
panel = MSC.panel_matrices(df, :county, :month, :unemployment_rate, :D)
```

This gives the same design counts as the CSV helper:

| quantity | value |
| --- | ---: |
| panel rows | 460,576 |
| counties | 3,112 |
| control counties | 438 |
| treated counties | 2,674 |
| months | 148 |
| pre-treatment months | 147 |

On my machine, materializing this panel took about 10.4 seconds with DuckDB and
about 23.1 seconds with the current CSV/DataFrames helper. The estimators are
not running inside DuckDB. DuckDB just does the wide-file scan, filtering,
complete-history check, and ordering before Julia receives the analysis table.

## Four estimators on the same outcome matrix

Now the same `Y`, `N0`, and `T0` can be passed to several estimators.

```julia
# Plain DiD
tau_did = SynthDiD.did_estimate(Y, N0, T0)

# Synthetic difference-in-differences
tau_sdid = SynthDiD.synthdid_estimate(Y, N0, T0)

# Synthetic control
tau_sc = SynthDiD.sc_estimate(Y, N0, T0)

# Multivariate synthetic control
tau_msc = MSC.msc_estimate(
    panel;
    lambdas = [0.03],
    standardize = false,
    max_iter = 100,
    tol = 1e-4,
)
```

On the downloaded BLS file, this gives:

| estimator | estimate |
| --- | ---: |
| Difference-in-differences | 2.6940 |
| Synthetic difference-in-differences | 2.6944 |
| Synthetic control | 3.4134 |
| Multivariate synthetic control | 4.9552 |
| Paper benchmark | about 5.06 |

These are not just four implementations of the same calculation. They make
different choices about which controls and which pre-periods matter.

## What changes across estimators?

Plain DiD uses equal unit weights and equal time weights. It asks whether
treated counties changed more from the pre-period average to April 2020 than
the no-order counties did. This is easy to understand, but it leans heavily on
a parallel-trends comparison between a very large treated group and seven
no-order states.

Synthetic control changes the unit weights. It tries to form a weighted control
group that better matches the treated group before April 2020. In this example
the estimate moves from about 2.69 to about 3.41 percentage points.

Synthetic DiD changes both unit and time weights. In this one-post-month
application, the SDiD estimate is almost the same as DiD. For this design, the
optimized weights do not move the simple average comparison much.

Multivariate synthetic control changes the target problem more. It does not fit
one synthetic control for an aggregate treated average, and it does not fit
2,674 separate synthetic controls. It learns a sparse matrix mapping 438
control counties to all 2,674 treated counties jointly, then averages the
treated-county effects. That is closer to the disaggregated problem in the
paper.

## What I learn from this

The estimates are not identical:

| comparison | lesson |
| --- | --- |
| DiD vs SC | unit weights matter |
| DiD vs SDiD | time weights may or may not matter in a one-post-period design |
| SC vs MSC | aggregate treated fit differs from high-dimensional treated-unit fit |
| MSC vs paper | matching sample counts is not the same as pinning the exact data vintage and optimizer |

For applied work, I think this is the right workflow. Start with one sample and
force the estimators to use it. Then disagreements are easier to interpret.

## Practical notes

The BLS data are large enough that I would not make the book download or parse
the file every time. The better pattern is:

1. keep the raw BLS flat file outside the book repository;
2. use DuckDB or a dedicated preparation script to produce a common panel object;
3. cache a small summary table of estimates;
4. make the chapter explain the design, code path, and interpretation.

The current `MSC.jl` example does this for the paper application. It looks for
`data/la.data.64.County` or an explicit `BLS_LAUS_COUNTY_FILE`, builds the
paper-sized panel, and prints the comparison with the reported paper number.
The DuckDB version above is just a faster way to do the same panel construction
when the full BLS flat file is available locally.

If the goal is exact reproduction of 5.06, the missing ingredient is not
another estimator. It is the paper's exact replication archive: the BLS vintage,
county inclusion file, and optimizer settings. Without that archive, I would
only claim that this replicates the application design and sample counts, and
then compares estimators on the same public data.
